item.title: Back to the future! Nvidia earnings/forecast lifts Nasdaq futures 1.3%
item.description:
The bounce in Nasdaq futures should spread to Asia’s chip supply chain, with Taiwan, South Korea and Japan’s semiconductor names the most direct beneficiaries of Nvidia’s comments on pricing and supply deals. The bigger test is whether the gains survive the US cash open, since after-hours rallies on single-stock news can fade once wider liquidity returns. The open governance issues are timed risks: Treasury Secretary Bessent’s 10-day deadline, the 10-Q filing due by early December and any update on the CEO search could each move the stock and, through it, the index. For now, traders have taken the demand story at face value.

---

Earlier:

  • Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
  • Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
  • SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
  • Nvidia board shuts the door on Huang’s return, refuses to discuss his exit on call
  • Nvidia sees 75% revenue growth next year as Kress points to $2.5 trillion backlog
  • Nvidia’s missing 10-Q: three reasons to be alert, not alarmed
  • Supplier, lender, shareholder: how Nvidia became the "Bank of AI"

---

Nvidia showed it can still turn the whole market on its own, but the rally rests on demand while the open questions are about leadership, regulators and paperwork.

Summary:

  • Nasdaq futures rose around 1.3% on Globex after Nvidia’s results and earnings call
  • Q3 revenue rose 103% to around $116 billion, ahead of forecasts, and Q4 is guided to $130 billion against estimates of about $125 billion
  • Interim CEO Colette Kress forecast about 75% revenue growth in fiscal 2028 and cited a $2.5 trillion cloud backlog
  • Nvidia plans to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders
  • The board ruled out Jensen Huang’s return and hired Heidrick & Struggles for the CEO search
  • A reported SEC probe, the delayed 10-Q and about $518 billion in commitments keep risks in view

Nasdaq futures rose around 1.3% on Globex after Nvidia’s results and earnings call, a reminder of how much weight a single company’s numbers can still carry for the wider market. The rebound follows a bruising November for AI stocks, with Nvidia’s own shares down about a quarter this month before the report.

The numbers that turned sentiment Nvidia beat forecasts across the board. Third-quarter revenue rose 103% from a year earlier to around $116 billion, against expectations of about $109 billion, and adjusted earnings came in at $2.68 a share. Fourth-quarter revenue is guided to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above estimates of about $125 billion.

The call did more to lift the mood. Interim chief executive Colette Kress said she expects revenue to grow about 75% in fiscal 2028 and pointed to a cloud-industry backlog of $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months earlier. Older chips are commanding higher prices, with Hopper contracts renewing at up to double their original level. Nvidia also said it intends to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders.

The governance overhang remains Chairman Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned last week, and has hired Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent chief executive. He declined to discuss Huang’s departure or the board’s investigation. Shares fell after hours at first, then recovered to trade nearly 3% higher during the call.

Other questions remain open. The Wall Street Journal reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants answers from the board within 10 days. Nvidia has also not yet filed its quarterly 10-Q alongside its results, breaking with its usual practice, although it has until early December.

The balance sheet story Nvidia’s role as a financier of the AI industry is also drawing attention. The Financial Times reported total commitments of about $518 billion, including $390 billion to lock in supply, mainly of memory chips. Receivables rose almost a third in the quarter to about $81 billion.

What comes next The futures rally shows the market wanted proof that AI demand is intact, and Nvidia supplied it. Whether the gains hold through the US cash session is another matter. Demand is no longer the main question for Nvidia. Leadership, regulators and the 10-Q are, and any of them could test the recovery in the days ahead.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Supplier, lender, shareholder: how Nvidia became the "Bank of AI"
item.description:
The commitments show how closely Nvidia’s fortunes are now tied to the financial health of AI labs and cloud providers, not just their appetite for chips. If funding conditions for those customers tighten, Nvidia faces exposure through unpaid bills and falling stake values as well as lost orders. Memory makers are the clearest beneficiaries of the $100 billion-plus jump in supply commitments, which gives them visibility on future demand. Expect analysts to track receivables and equity gains as closely as revenue from here.

---

So far today:

  • Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
  • Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
  • SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
  • Nvidia board shuts the door on Huang’s return, refuses to discuss his exit on call
  • Nvidia sees 75% revenue growth next year as Kress points to $2.5 trillion backlog
  • Nvidia’s missing 10-Q: three reasons to be alert, not alarmed

---

Nvidia no longer just sells the AI boom its chips: it underwrites suppliers, invests in customers and waits longer to be paid, which makes its balance sheet as important as its revenue line.

Summary:

  • Nvidia’s total commitments, including supply, equity investments, cloud services and leases, reached about $518 billion
  • Supply chain commitments rose more than $100 billion in three months to $390 billion, mainly for memory chips
  • Equity holdings have roughly tripled since January, and Nvidia has spent about $58 billion on stakes this fiscal year
  • Receivables rose almost a third from the previous quarter to about $81 billion, faster than revenue
  • Free cash flow of about $44 billion in the quarter gives Nvidia ample room to fund this

Nvidia’s quarterly results are usually read as a scorecard for AI chip demand. This time the balance sheet tells a second story: Nvidia is increasingly acting as a lender, investor and guaranteed buyer for the AI industry, not just its main supplier.

Half a trillion dollars in commitments Nvidia said on Tuesday it had made more than half a trillion dollars in financial commitments, the Financial Times reported. That includes $390 billion in supply chain commitments, up more than $100 billion in three months, mainly to secure memory chips. Add equity investments, cloud services and data centre leases, and the total reaches about $518 billion.

Locking in supply on that scale works much like a bank extending credit. Nvidia is guaranteeing future orders to its suppliers, which helps them fund new capacity.

Investing in its own customers The balance sheet shows how fast Nvidia’s investment book has grown. Holdings of non-marketable securities, largely stakes in private companies, rose to about $66 billion from around $22 billion in January. Listed equity holdings climbed to about $44 billion from roughly $13 billion. Nvidia spent about $58 billion buying equity stakes in the first nine months of the fiscal year. Many of those investments are in AI labs and cloud providers that also buy Nvidia chips.

Customers owe more Accounts receivable, the money customers owe for products already delivered, reached about $81 billion, up almost a third from three months earlier, according to the FT. That is faster than revenue growth of 20% over the same period.

Why be alert, but not alarmed Critics call this circular financing: Nvidia funds customers who then buy its chips, which flatters demand. The risk is real if those customers struggle to pay or to raise money. But Nvidia generated about $44 billion of free cash flow in the quarter and has said it will return all excess cash to shareholders. For now it is financing the AI build-out from strength, not stretching to keep it going. The question to watch is whether receivables and investments keep outpacing sales. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia’s missing 10-Q: three reasons to be alert, not alarmed
item.description:
A delayed 10-Q keeps the governance overhang alive but does not undermine the reported numbers. A missed deadline or new legal disclosures would be the real trigger for selling.

---

So far:

  • Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
  • Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
  • SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
  • Nvidia board shuts the door on Huang’s return, refuses to discuss his exit on call
  • Nvidia sees 75% revenue growth next year as Kress points to $2.5 trillion backlog

---

Nvidia’s late paperwork is worth watching, but it says nothing bad about the numbers.

Summary:

  • Nvidia did not file its 10-Q with its results, breaking with recent practice
  • Its own release flagged the 10-Q in forward-looking statements
  • The deadline is around 4 December
  • A missed deadline or new control or legal disclosures would be the real warning signs

Nvidia has not filed its quarterly 10-Q alongside its third-quarter results, breaking with recent practice. Social media posts claim this makes the numbers meaningless. That goes too far, but three points are well worth watching. Let's briefly highlight these:

1. Late against habit, not the law Nvidia filed its last two 10-Qs on results day. Large companies have 40 days after quarter end, giving Nvidia until around 4 December.

2. Nvidia flagged it Its release today listed the 10-Q among forward-looking statements, alongside the CEO search and the board investigation, suggesting the delay was expected.

3. The figures stand for now Results are unaudited at this stage anyway. Real warning signs would be a missed deadline, a control weakness or new legal disclosures on Asia sales, with interim chief Colette Kress now personally certifying the filing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia sees 75% revenue growth next year as Kress points to $2.5 trillion backlog
item.description:
A forecast of about 75% growth next year directly answers the worry that has weighed on AI stocks for the past month, which is that demand is peaking. The call turned sentiment, with the shares recovering from early after-hours losses to trade nearly 3% higher. The pledge to return all excess free cash flow adds a floor of support from buybacks for a stock still carrying a governance discount. Rising prices for older chips are a strong signal for the wider AI hardware chain, from memory makers to the Asian packaging and substrate suppliers Nvidia named. That should support semiconductor names across Taiwan, South Korea and Japan in the session ahead.

---

The earnings coverage so far:

  • Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
  • Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
  • SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
  • Nvidia board shuts the door on Huang’s return, refuses to discuss his exit on call

---

Kress used her first call as interim chief to argue that Nvidia’s growth story is accelerating, and she backed it with higher chip prices and a promise to hand back every spare dollar of cash.

Summary:

  • Kress expects revenue to grow about 75% in fiscal 2028, with enterprise revenue more than doubling
  • The cloud-industry backlog has reached $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months ago
  • Hopper contracts are renewing at up to twice the original price, and B300 prices are up more than 60% since launch
  • Purchase commitments rose to $390 billion in Q3. Nvidia signed new supply deals, and its roadmap is unchanged, with Vera Rubin Ultra due next year and Feynman in 2028
  • Nvidia returned a record $28 billion in Q3 and plans to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders
  • Heidrick & Struggles will lead the CEO search, and the board ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang

Nvidia expects revenue to grow about 75% in fiscal 2028, interim chief executive Colette Kress told analysts on the company’s earnings call. It was her first outlook since taking over from Jensen Huang, and it was emphatic. She also expects enterprise revenue to more than double over the year.

Kress pointed to a cloud-industry backlog of $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months earlier, as evidence that demand is still building. Pricing backs that up. She said Hopper GPU contracts, an older generation, have been renewed under multi-year agreements at prices up to double their original level. Prices for the newer B300 have risen more than 60% since launch, and GPU rental rates have climbed across all generations. Older hardware gaining value is unusual in the chip industry, and it suggests compute is still in short supply.

Usage is rising as well. Kress said token prices, the cost of running AI models, have fallen nearly 60% since May, which has accelerated usage and demand for compute. Agentic workloads now make up about 80% of all tokens. She expects major frontier labs to account for about 15% of data centre revenue this year.

Nvidia is spending heavily to meet that demand. Purchase commitments rose to $390 billion in the third quarter, and commitments tied to neocloud agreements reached $32 billion. Kress announced new substrate agreements with Kinsus Technology and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and an advanced-packaging deal with Siliconware Precision Industries. She also said Nvidia would stay cautious and disciplined in its capital commitments. The product roadmap is unchanged, with Vera Rubin Ultra still expected to launch next year and the Feynman architecture to follow in 2028.

Kress also signalled a more generous approach to shareholder returns. Nvidia returned a record $28 billion in the third quarter, about $22 billion through buybacks and $6 billion in dividends, and has handed back around 65% of free cash flow so far this year. From here, she said, the company intends to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders.

Leadership was addressed briefly. Chairman Harvey Jones said the board has no plans to reinstate Huang and has hired Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search for a permanent chief executive. He declined to discuss Huang’s resignation or the board’s ongoing investigation. Kress said Nvidia’s commitments to customers and partners would not change.

The shares swung during the call, recovering early after-hours losses to trade nearly 3% higher. The 75% forecast sets a high bar for a company still without a permanent leader, but on this call, demand rather than governance drove the share price.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia board shuts the door on Huang’s return, refuses to discuss his exit on call
item.description:
The share dip shows investors care about leadership. A strong beat and higher guidance were not enough to hold the early after-hours gains once the board ruled out Huang’s return (note that investors are fickle and the move can be easily reversed and reversed again etc. in thin after hours trade). That removes a comeback scenario some shareholders had been hoping for and leaves Nvidia with an interim chief executive, no named successor and an investigation it won’t discuss. With an SEC probe reported and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent seeking answers from the board within 10 days, the governance discount on the stock could persist even as the AI demand story stays intact. Weakness in Nvidia could weigh on the wider AI trade and Asian chip names in the session ahead.

--

Nvidia’s board used its first earnings call without Jensen Huang to close the door on his return, and investors liked that less than they liked the numbers.

Summary:

  • Chairman Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
  • Jones said the board would communicate further when appropriate
  • The company said it would not take questions on the circumstances of Huang’s resignation
  • Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be honoured to return as chief executive
  • Nvidia shares turned lower after hours despite beating forecasts and guiding fourth-quarter revenue above estimates
  • Colette Kress remains interim CEO while the board’s independent investigation continues

Nvidia’s board has ruled out bringing back Jensen Huang as chief executive. Board chairman Harvey Jones told analysts on the company’s earnings call that directors do not intend to reinstate him, and that the board would communicate further when appropriate.

Nvidia also said it would not take questions about the circumstances of Huang’s resignation. That left analysts unable to explore the issue that has dominated the company for the past week, on a call that would normally focus on record AI chip demand.

Nvidia shares swung sharply in after-hours trading, falling at first before recovering to trade nearly 3% higher during the call. Investors were weighing results that comfortably beat forecasts, with third-quarter revenue of around $116 billion and fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion.

The board’s position contrasts with comments from Huang himself. Earlier on Tuesday, he said in a statement, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, that he would be honoured to return as chief executive. Sources had already told CNBC on Monday that the board was not considering reinstating him. The call made that position official.

Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director on 12 November. His departure followed the opening of a board investigation into his disclosure of a relationship with a business executive accused of being a Chinese spy. The independent board committee leading that investigation is still at work, and finance chief Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive. Jones said the company has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search for a permanent chief executive.

Pressure is also building from outside the company. The Wall Street Journal has reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said he wants answers from the board within 10 days. Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia’s board also created a committee to oversee national security and export control compliance.

The board has now settled one question but left several others open. Investors have no timeline for a permanent chief executive, no findings from the investigation, and no detail on what regulators are examining. Until those answers come, the strength of Nvidia’s business may not be enough on its own to steady the stock.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
item.description:
The probe adds a fresh regulatory overhang just as the earnings beat gives the shares some relief, and it may limit how much of that rally holds. A disclosure investigation goes to the heart of how far investors can trust Nvidia’s reported numbers, particularly in Asia, where its sales have been strongest outside the US. Any evidence that chips were diverted to China would raise the risk of tighter export controls across Southeast Asia, a threat to Nvidia’s guidance and to the regional data centre build-out that supports Asian chip and server suppliers. Expect analysts to press interim CEO Colette Kress on the probe during the conference call.

---

Nvidia’s crisis has moved from the boardroom to the regulators, and the question now is whether its Asia sales figures told investors the whole story.

Summary:

  • The SEC has opened a civil investigation into Nvidia, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported, citing people familiar with the matter
  • The probe includes whether the company’s disclosures misled investors
  • Jensen Huang resigned as CEO after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and one with an employee
  • Nvidia had earlier denied any unusual relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which was suspected of diverting chips to China
  • Nvidia stopped disclosing its Singapore sales last year
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has asked for answers from the board and outside counsel within 10 days

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia following the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The newspaper said the civil probe includes whether the chipmaker’s disclosures misled investors, although its full scope could not be determined.

Huang stepped down after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee, according to the Journal. Nvidia shares have fallen more than 10% since he was ousted.

The case has drawn attention to Alice Huang, then an executive at the Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials believe is working for China’s intelligence services. China has denied the allegation. Earlier this year, Nvidia denied that Jensen Huang had any unusual or unexpected relationship with her. Megaspeed was one of several companies using Nvidia chips to build AI data centres in Southeast Asia, and was suspected of diverting some of those products to China. The Commerce Department had been investigating it since late 2024, and the Journal has reported that the Justice Department is now leading several investigations involving Alice Huang.

Disclosure is a sensitive point. The Journal noted that Nvidia changed how it reports international chip sales last year, dropping a breakdown that showed its sales to Singapore, where Megaspeed was based.

Pressure from Washington is building. Congress has called for investigations, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week questioned whether Nvidia knowingly sold powerful chips to China to boost its earnings. He said he wanted answers from the board and its outside counsel within 10 days. In a statement on Tuesday, Huang said he had fallen short of the standards expected at Nvidia and took full responsibility for his mistakes.

The report landed hours before Nvidia posted quarterly results well ahead of forecasts. On the same day, the company also set up a board committee to oversee national security and export control compliance. Strong numbers may steady the stock for now, but investors are likely to weigh any revenue upside against the risk that regulators find problems in how Nvidia has accounted for and disclosed its sales in Asia. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
item.description:
The committee is unlikely to move the shares much, since the earnings beat is driving overnight trade. Its value is in reducing tail risk: a formal board-level response could help calm regulators and lawmakers who have been pressing Nvidia since the Huang scandal broke. Export policy is still the biggest swing factor for Nvidia’s China exposure and for the Asian chip supply chain around it, so traders will read the move as an attempt to protect licences and political goodwill. The real test will be the findings of the board investigation, not this structure.

---

Just out:

  • Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit

---

Nvidia is putting national security oversight in the boardroom, a message aimed squarely at Washington as it tries to move past its founder’s sudden exit.

Summary:

  • Nvidia’s board has created the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee as a new standing committee
  • Director Suzanne Nora Johnson chairs it, with directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members
  • The committee will meet at least quarterly and retain independent experts in law, national security and trade compliance
  • Nvidia’s National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the committee, and to interim CEO Colette Kress on day-to-day operations
  • Chairman Harvey Jones said advanced chips and AI pose unprecedented national security challenges
  • The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO; the release does not mention him

Nvidia’s board has set up a standing committee to oversee the chipmaker’s national security policies and export control compliance. The step comes less than a week after founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive.

Director Suzanne Nora Johnson will chair the new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, with directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia said in a statement that the committee will meet at least quarterly, both with management and in executive session. It will also retain independent outside experts in law, national security and trade compliance.

Nvidia’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will now report directly to the committee, as well as to interim chief executive Colette Kress for day-to-day operations. The committee will also oversee efforts to strengthen both teams.

Board chairman Harvey Jones said advanced chips and the rise of artificial intelligence and superintelligence present national security challenges without precedent. He said that as the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has a responsibility to help lead the industry’s response. He added that the company wants to work with government and industry on a framework that protects national security while still allowing innovation. Nvidia said the move reflects the board’s commitment to closer engagement with government stakeholders and to high standards of governance.

The statement does not mention Huang. He stepped down on 12 November after the board opened an investigation into his disclosure of a relationship with a business executive accused of being a Chinese spy, which China denies. That investigation, led by an independent board committee, is ongoing, and US lawmakers have demanded answers.

The announcement came on the same day Nvidia reported quarterly results well ahead of forecasts. The company guided to around $130 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, again assuming no data centre compute sales to China.

For investors, the committee matters less for the numbers than for the company’s standing in Washington. Nvidia’s business depends heavily on export licences and political goodwill, and the board appears keen to show that oversight of sensitive trade now sits at the top of the company. Whether that settles concerns will depend on what the investigation finds and on who becomes the permanent chief executive. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
item.description:
A clean beat on revenue, earnings and guidance should give the bruised AI trade a lift into the Asian session. Nasdaq futures and Asia’s chip supply chain, including TSMC, SK Hynix, Samsung and Advantest, are the obvious beneficiaries. Nvidia shares rose in early after-hours trade, but the move so far is modest next to the roughly 8% swing options had priced. That suggests traders are holding back until the conference call. Lower gross margin guidance and open questions about leadership and the board investigation could cap any rally if Kress gives an unconvincing account of either.

---

Nvidia’s numbers answered the demand question emphatically, which leaves the boardroom as the only real doubt hanging over the stock.

Summary:

  • Fiscal Q3 revenue rose 103% from a year earlier to around $116 billion, against expectations of about $109 billion
  • Adjusted EPS was $2.68, against forecasts of about $2.48
  • Data centre revenue more than doubled to around $108 billion, against a consensus of about $102 billion
  • Q4 revenue is guided to $130 billion plus or minus 3%, against estimates of about $125 billion. The quarter includes an extra week, and no China data centre compute sales are assumed
  • Q4 gross margins are guided to 71% to 72%, down from around 75% in Q3
  • This is the first report under interim CEO Colette Kress, who replaced Jensen Huang after his resignation on 12 November

Nvidia beat Wall Street forecasts on revenue, earnings and guidance in its first quarterly report since founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive. The results offer investors some reassurance after a bruising month for the stock.

Revenue for the fiscal third quarter, which ended 25 October, rose 103% from a year earlier to around $116 billion. That was comfortably ahead of the roughly $109 billion analysts had expected. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.68 a share, against forecasts of about $2.48. Data centre revenue, which makes up almost all of Nvidia’s sales, more than doubled to around $108 billion, well above a consensus of about $102 billion.

The outlook was stronger still. Nvidia said in its earnings release that it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, against estimates of about $125 billion. The quarter includes an extra week, which flatters the comparison somewhat, and the company again assumed no data centre compute sales to China. Gross margins are guided to 71% to 72%, down from around 75% in the third quarter. That is a step lower that analysts are likely to press management on.

Colette Kress, interim chief executive and still the finance chief, said the company’s momentum was real. She described the start of the new Vera Rubin platform as explosive. Nvidia said Vera Rubin NVL72 systems have shipped in the fastest product ramp in its history, with racks already running at major cloud providers including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

Nvidia returned about $28 billion to shareholders during the quarter. It has about $227 billion left under its buyback authorisation after the board added $150 billion in September.

The backdrop is unusual. Huang stepped down on 12 November. His resignation followed a board investigation, launched after he disclosed a relationship with a business executive accused of being a Chinese spy. The risk language in the release refers to the leadership transition, the search for a new chief executive and an ongoing review by an independent board committee. The stock had fallen about 24% in November before the report.

The question now is whether results this strong can separate the business from the boardroom. Demand for Nvidia’s chips looks firmly intact. Investors will focus on what Kress says about margins, the CEO search and the investigation, where any surprise could matter more than the quarter itself.  

ADDED:

Cash generation was just as strong. Free cash flow came to around $44 billion in the quarter, about double the level a year earlier. Nvidia also pointed to an agreement to acquire Hugging Face, the AI model platform, and said it had expanded Anthropic’s access to its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers. Meta plans a wider rollout of Vera Rubin systems.

Bueller ... Bueller .... Bueller?

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks fall; Dow stocks are the hardest hit with a drop of 1.65%
item.description:
US stocks closed lower across the board, with the Dow Industrial Average leading the declines. Salesforce was a big drain, falling 9.41%, but the selling extended well beyond one stock. Twenty-five of the Dow’s 30 components finished lower.

Small caps also struggled, with the Russell 2000 losing 1.50%. The Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 held up better on a relative basis, but both still closed lower by roughly 0.7%. There was little comfort for buyers in the closing numbers.

During the session, reports of communications disruptions added uncertainty and coincided with flight-to-safety flows into Treasuries, gold, the CHF and JPY. Those were intraday moves; they did not prevent another lower close for stocks. images.investinglive.com

US closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average: −849.06 points (−1.65%) to 50,764.09.
  • S&P 500: −76.06 points (−1.03%) to 7,340.53.
  • Nasdaq Composite: −181.37 points (−0.74%) to 24,328.38.
  • Russell 2000: −41.07 points (−1.50%) to 2,701.87.
  • Nasdaq 100: −195.37 points (−0.72%) to 27,001.78.

Salesforce leads the Dow percentage losers

Salesforce fell $20.21 to $194.62, closing near its session low of $193.41. Salesforce plunged 9.41% as software shares came under heavy selling pressure. A string of technology outages heightened concerns about software reliability and security, while competition from AI-native platforms remained an overhang. Salesforce has not been publicly linked to the reported disruptions. Technically, the price fell below both its 100 and 200 day MAs adding to the bearish bias.  

Other sizable Dow losses included:

  • Nike: −6.30% to $35.85.
  • UnitedHealth: −5.39% to $389.81.
  • IBM: −4.69% to $231.14.
  • JPMorgan Chase: −2.43% to $329.99.
  • Home Depot: −2.40% to $339.17.

  • Visa: −2.23% to $416.97.

The weakness reached across software, healthcare, financials and consumer shares. That breadth matters. Salesforce was a standout loser, but the Dow’s decline had plenty of participation.

Only five Dow stocks finish higher

The winners were few, and their gains were modest:

  • Cisco: +0.62% to $95.11.
  • Honeywell: +0.46% to $218.96.
  • McDonald’s: +0.39% to $275.73.

Among other large technology names, Apple slipped 0.25% and Nvidia fell 0.48%. Those declines were relatively contained compared with Salesforce and Microsoft, helping explain some of the Nasdaq’s relative resilience.

Other notable losers

Selling also hit software, travel, solar and consumer-related shares:

For traders, the index is a useful barometer, but look underneath it. With 25 Dow stocks declining and the five winners posting only small gains, the closing weakness extended well beyond the headline loser.

Meanwhile .... a preview of the data calendar due today in Asia-Pacific:

Australian wage data due as markets bet against a December RBA hike

Australia’s September quarter wage figures, due from the Australian Bureau of Statistics at 11.30am Sydney time (0030 GMT), arrive a day after the Reserve Bank of Australia sounded more hawkish than markets expected.

Consensus expects the Wage Price Index to rise 1.0% in the quarter. That would be a step up from 0.8%, the pace recorded for five straight quarters. Annual growth is forecast at 3.4%, up from 3.2%.

The expected pick-up has an obvious cause. The Fair Work Commission’s annual review delivered a larger than expected 4.75% increase in award wages, and most of those rises pass through in the September quarter, when the new financial year begins. The real question is whether the gains reach beyond award-reliant workers. Private sector wage growth had slowed to its softest pace since late 2021, and Commonwealth Bank’s own tracking shows pay has not materially responded to higher inflation.

The RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.85% earlier this month, its fifth hike this year and an 18-year high. The board was split 6-3. Minutes released on Tuesday showed the majority judged that rates were not clearly sufficient to bring inflation under control. The three dissenters warned the economy may be nearing a sharper downturn. Governor Michele Bullock said the same day that inflation risks remain skewed to the upside.

Markets have all but priced out a December move, and today’s release tests that view. A 1.0% result would largely confirm the award-wage effect and probably leave pricing little changed. A stronger number, especially one showing broad private sector gains, could lift the Australian dollar and short-dated yields as traders reconsider. A softer print would back the dissenters.

The wider labour market argues against a lasting wage surge. Unemployment has risen to 4.7% and job advertisements are declining, while wage growth still trails inflation.

item.title: Fed's Williams: The economy is getting stronger, inflation not moving in the right direction
item.description:
New York Fed President John Williams is out with some fresh commentary, and the message is a classic mix of acknowledging the inflation headache while trying to keep the market from pricing in anything too aggressive.

  • I don't think the situation calls for dramatic policy action

  • Tariffs and energy shock still affecting inflation readings

  • Is seeing signs of shocks spilling over into broader inflation data

  • Inflation is 'stubbornly high'

  • Fed still has more work to do to get inflation back to 2%

  • The economy is strong and getting stronger, inflation is not moving in right direction

The big takeaway here for traders is that line about avoiding "dramatic policy action." Coming off the back of this week's hot October CPI print—and with the market increasingly jittery about the Fed having to ramp up its hiking cycle after restarting it in September—Williams is effectively pouring cold water on the idea of a 50 bps move.

Still, you can't ignore the hawkish undertones. Admitting that tariff and energy shocks are spilling over into the broader data is a notable shift. Back in October, Williams was singing a much more patient tune, arguing there was "no need for urgency" ahead of the late-October FOMC meeting and suggesting he saw no need for hikes in 2027. While he was open to one more quarter-point hike before year-end back then, the tone today is noticeably more concerned about the stickiness of prices—even if he isn't ready to panic.

For the December 9 decision, a 25 bps hike remains the clear base case and it's fully priced into markets with a dwindling chance of 50 bps.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why Warren Buffet and Berkshire Hathaway keep going back to airlines
item.description:
Berkshire Hathaway is buying more Delta Air Lines and I think there's a fascinating story behind why Warren Buffett and his successors keep getting drawn back into the airline business.

Berkshire's latest 13F filing, released late Monday, showed it increased its stake in Delta by 7.13 million shares in the third quarter, or 12.4%, bringing its total holdings to 64.45 million shares, or nearly 10% of the company.

That's the third consecutive quarter Berkshire has built its position. It started with 39.8 million shares at the end of March, increased that to 57.3 million in June and has now added another 7.1 million.

This isn't a small position anymore, and the steady accumulation suggests growing conviction even as the war in Iran and fuel price spike have hurt airline economics.

What's particularly interesting is Berkshire's long and tortured history with airlines.

Buffett famously described himself as an "aeroholic" and joked about having a telephone hotline to stop him from buying airline stocks. He also repeated the old joke that the fastest way to become a millionaire was to start as a billionaire and buy an airline.

In his 2007 shareholder letter, he described airlines as the worst kind of business: one that grows rapidly, requires enormous amounts of capital and ultimately earns little or nothing.

Yet Berkshire keeps buying them.

Buffett invested in USAir in 1989, bought major stakes in the four largest US airlines beginning in 2016 and sold them all during the pandemic in 2020 at the bottom. Now Berkshire is back again.

To me, people have always misunderstood Buffett's airline comments.

The aeroholic joke isn't really about hating airlines. It's about loving them too much. Buffett keeps finding reasons to invest in the industry, only to be disappointed by its economics.

And it's easy to understand the attraction.

Airlines have enormous barriers to entry, irreplaceable airport infrastructure, powerful networks and a service that people will continue to need for generations. There is no risk from AI. There is tremendous operating leverage in filling an additional seat on an aircraft that's already scheduled to fly.

Those are precisely the kinds of characteristics that Buffett has spent his career looking for. He likes companies with durable demand, economies of scale, formidable competitive positions and pricing power.

Airlines appear to possess the first three in abundance. Their historical problem is that the fourth — pricing power — has frequently disappeared when competitors added too much capacity.

But what if that's changing?

The railroad comparison

There's a fascinating parallel with another industry that Buffett once avoided: railroads.

For much of their history, railroads were terrible investments. They were capital-intensive, heavily unionized, intensely competitive and chronically unable to earn adequate returns.

Then the industry consolidated, deregulation allowed companies to rationalize their networks, and the economics fundamentally changed.

The tracks were still expensive. The trains still required maintenance. The workers still needed to be paid. But an industry that had destroyed capital for generations suddenly became a tremendous business and a famously good investment for 30 years.

Buffett eventually recognized that transformation as he bought shares Norfold Southern and Union Pacific. Then Berkshire acquired BNSF in 2010 for $44 billion in what was his largest ever acquisition.

Charlie Munger explicitly made the airline comparison at the 2017 Berkshire annual meeting:

"You've got to remember that the railroads were a terrible business for decades and decades and decades and then they got good."

At the Daily Journal meeting that same year, Munger went further, saying that railroads had been terrible for about 80 years before consolidation improved the business, and that something similar was happening in airlines.

That's the part of the Buffett and Munger airline story that tends to get overlooked.

They weren't necessarily saying airlines would always be terrible investments. They were recognizing that an industry with attractive underlying characteristics could eventually develop attractive economics.

The US airline industry has already consolidated dramatically, and there are signs that carriers are increasingly prioritizing profitability over market share.

Delta might be the clearest example.

Delta is becoming a different kind of business

Delta's third-quarter results showed premium ticket revenue rising 18% from a year earlier, reaching $6.82 billion and overtaking main cabin ticket revenue.

Meanwhile, its relationship with American Express continues to become more valuable. Delta expects to receive more than $9 billion in remuneration from American Express this year, supported by its SkyMiles loyalty ecosystem.

Those payments aren't pure profit, but they represent an increasingly important revenue stream tied to customer loyalty and spending rather than simply selling airline seats.

Delta also benefits from dominant hub positions, a premium brand and a customer base that is increasingly willing to pay more for a better travel experience.

It's not difficult to imagine why Berkshire would find those characteristics attractive, particularly given its long history as a major American Express shareholder (perhaps offering visibility into why the partnership works so well for AXP).

The remaining question is whether the industry can sustain that profitability through the next downturn.

Fuel prices, labour costs, aircraft purchases and economic shocks haven't gone away. Airlines still have the ability to undermine one another by adding too much capacity, though I would argue that the wave of new entrants into the space is a thing of the past following the bust of most discount airlines.

Importantly, the distinction from railroads matters. A railroad owns a largely irreplaceable network of tracks, while aircraft can be moved into profitable markets by competitors.

Still, the possibility of a structural transformation is intriguing.

The valuation opportunity

The four major publicly traded North American railroads generally trade around 20–24 times forward earnings, compared with roughly 13 times for Delta.

That's an enormous valuation gap.

If Delta could demonstrate railroad-like durability in its earnings and attract a 20-times multiple on $7.50 in normalized annual earnings per share, the stock would be worth $150, compared with approximately $87 today.

At $9 in annual earnings and the same multiple, it would be worth $180.

Those are illustrative scenarios rather than price targets, and there's no guarantee airlines will ever deserve railroad valuations.

But they show the potential rewards if investors eventually stop thinking about airlines as permanently bad businesses and begin valuing their competitive advantages.

There's one final wrinkle in the Berkshire story. Buffett told the Wall Street Journal in May that he wasn't involved in the renewed Delta investment. Greg Abel became Berkshire's CEO at the beginning of 2026, and the company hasn't publicly identified who directed the subsequent purchases.

So this may not be Buffett himself returning to an old obsession but the investment fits a question that he and Munger wrestled with for decades: Can an industry that has historically destroyed shareholder capital eventually become a wonderful business?

Railroads proved that it can.

And judging by Berkshire's steadily growing investment in Delta, somebody in Omaha thinks airlines might finally be getting there.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia earnings after the close. The price is testing a key downside target. What are the key levels for traders?
item.description:
Shares of Nvidia reached a all-time high price of $243.37 back on October 5. Since then, the price has fallen by -$94.57 or -38.86% to a cycle lows reached last week on November 12 at $148.80. Today, the price retested that low level reaching a low price of $150.37 before bouncing modestly to the upside.  The price currently trading at $153.82.

Nvidia reports its fiscal third-quarter results after the close today, with shares testing a key downside swing area between $146.50 and $151.84. Buyers will be looking for the earnings and outlook to help stabilize the price. Sellers will be looking for another reason to push through support.

The earnings expectations show how much growth is already anticipated:

  • Adjusted earnings per share: $2.47 expected versus $1.30 originally reported a year ago, an increase of 90%.
  • Revenue: $108.72 billion expected versus $57.01 billion a year ago, an increase of approximately 90.7%. Him him

Estimates vary slightly by provider, but the broad expectation is for Nvidia to nearly double both earnings and revenue compared with a year ago. The company’s own revenue guidance was $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, with gross margins projected at 74%, plus or minus half a percentage point. NVIDIA Newsroom

The forward guidance will be a major barometer. For the next quarter, analysts are looking for earnings of $2.73 per share and revenue of $124.69 billion. Traders will compare Nvidia’s outlook with those expectations to judge whether the growth story remains on track. Despite the sharp

Despite the sharp rise in both EPS and revenues from year ago levels, the price of Nvidia is down from about $186 from year ago levels, to the current price near $153.50. The declines are being driven by expectations of slower AI growth ahead and also by the company specific news of Jensen Huang being ousted as a CEO and board member.  Technically, the price is also suffered setbacks. 

What are the technicals telling traders?

Nvidia’s 4-hour chart shows the price testing a key support area near $146.50–$151.90 heading into earnings. That area is the immediate barometer for buyers and sellers.

A former ceiling is being tested as a floor.

The zone acted as a ceiling from November 2024 through June 2025. Once buyers broke above it, the price extended higher, eventually reaching its all-time high in October. The subsequent decline has brought Nvidia back to that former ceiling. Can it now hold as a floor?

The technical breaks keep sellers in control.

The technical damage on the way down has been significant. Shares have broken below the 100-day moving average at $211.47 and the 200-day moving average at $203.86. Sellers have also pushed through the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the 2025 low at $183.49 and the 50% midpoint near $165.

That midpoint sits within a swing area between $164.07 and $168.80. For buyers, that zone is now a key upside hurdle. Getting above it—and staying above it—would be an initial step toward repairing the technical damage. Until then, sellers remain firmly in control, even if the price rebounds from support.

The $146.50 level defines the downside risk.

The lows from last week and this week near $150 have stalled within the longer-term swing area between $146.53 and $151.90. The 61.8% retracement at $146.50 reinforces the lower boundary, creating a clear level for traders to define risk.

With shares near $153.50, buyers are attempting to bounce from that support zone for the second time in a week. That makes the area especially important through the earnings release.

Hold above it, and buyers retain a foundation for a recovery. Break below $146.50 and stay below, and another layer of support gives way, opening the door toward the $130 area.

Buyers need to reclaim $164.07–$168.80.

A move above the $164.07–$168.80 resistance zone would give buyers more technical support and shift attention toward $183.49–$189.80.

The levels define the roadmap. Earnings will provide the next test. Buyers need to defend support and reclaim resistance. Sellers still have control until the price action proves otherwise.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Flight to safety concerns from continued cyber issues send stocks lower, yields lower, gold higher, JPY and CHF up
item.description:
Reports that the National Security Agency’s internal communications network is down have added uncertainty to trading. Reuters, citing CNN, reports that the scope is being investigated, with no immediate evidence of a cyberattack. reuters.com

There are also reports circulating about possible Gmail and Microsoft Outlook disruptions, although a fresh widespread outage has not been confirmed. Google’s status dashboard currently lists no incidents. google.com

The market reaction has been a move toward safety. Stocks have moved lower, gold has pushed higher, Treasury yields have backed away from their highs, and buyers have moved into the CHF and JPY.

But have the technicals done enough to confirm that shift?

Nasdaq breaks below its 50% midpoint

The NASDAQ composite has fallen below 24,206.50, the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the end-of-March low to the October high.

That gives sellers another technical break to build on. Staying below the midpoint keeps the sellers more in control. Moving back above would take some of the pressure off and raise the risk of a failed break.

For now, that level becomes a close barometer for buyers and sellers.

Gold moves higher but still faces resistance

Gold extended to a session high of $3,891.07, but remains below its falling 100 hour moving average at $3,906.46.

The flight-to-safety buying has helped. However, if the price is going higher, buyers need to get and stay above that moving average.

Until that happens, sellers still have a level to lean against. A sustained break above would give buyers more control and strengthen the technical case for a further recovery.

Treasury yields retreat, but support remains intact

The US 10 year yield moved from a high near 5.158% to a low of 5.093% as Treasury buying picked up.

However, the yield remains above its rising 100 hour moving average at 5.087%. That is the first downside hurdle. Below that, the swing area between 5.00% and 5.03% becomes the next key target.

Those levels need to be broken to take more of the upside pressure off yields. The retreat is a step lower, but the technical picture has more work to do.

Inflation concerns also remain part of the backdrop following the import and export price data released earlier today.

CHF and JPY attract haven demand

The CHF and JPY have attracted buying against the USD over the last hour of trading as traders move toward traditional safe-haven currencies.

In the video above, I take a look at the technicals across these markets and explain the bias, the risks and the targets given the price action.

The trading lesson: Headlines create the move. Technicals define the risk.

A headline can change sentiment quickly. The technical levels help traders judge whether that initial reaction is gaining traction.

For the NASDAQ, the question is whether sellers can keep the price below its 50% midpoint. For gold, buyers need to clear the 100 hour moving average. For the 10 year yield, a break below its own 100 hour moving average would strengthen the move lower.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq stretching toward the swing area and 50% retracement targets. Key support being tested.

item.title: US Sept business inventories +0.5% vs +0.4% prior
item.description:
• Prior was +0.4%
  • Retail inventories ex-autos +0.5% vs +0.4% prior

This report is rarely a market mover but it's an input into GDP, so a strong number will boost tracking estimates and vice versa.

For background, the Census Bureau’s Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales report, known as business inventories, is released monthly at 10 am ET about six weeks after the reference month ends. It combines inventories and sales across the three main stages of the goods supply chain: manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers.

Much of the report is known by the time it’s released. Manufacturing inventories come out in the factory orders report, and advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories are published about two weeks earlier in the Advance Economic Indicators release. Business inventories adds the full retail figures and pulls everything into a combined total, so the headline change in total business inventories rarely surprises.

Retail inventories are the most useful piece. They’re broken down by type of store, including motor vehicle and parts dealers, general merchandise, food and beverage stores, clothing, furniture and building materials. Auto dealer inventories swing sharply with production schedules, supply disruptions and incentives, so economists focus on retail inventories excluding autos. That measure feeds directly into the inventory investment component of GDP and often prompts revisions to growth estimates.

The report also includes inventory-to-sales ratios for each sector and in total. A rising ratio can mean demand is softening and stock is piling up, or that businesses are deliberately building buffers. A falling ratio points to lean shelves and the potential for restocking, which can support future production. The figures are in nominal dollars, so higher prices can lift inventory values without any change in physical stock.

Inventories have become a bigger swing factor in recent years. Tariff-driven stockpiling followed by drawdowns has created large distortions in quarterly GDP, making the retail detail more relevant than usual.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Home Depot earnings offer a mixed picture of the US consumer as spending improves but traffic remains weak
item.description:
Home Depot reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and sales on Tuesday but shares fell 1.9% in premarket trading as the company faces margin pressure. It's the first of the major retailers to report this week.

The home improvement giant reported adjusted earnings of $3.86 per share compared to $3.84 expected, while revenue of $43.4 billion topped the $42.8 billion consensus.

The more interesting numbers are buried deeper in the report and offer some clues about the health of the US consumer.

Comparable sales rose 2.2% in the quarter, including a matching 2.2% increase in the US. That's an improvement from the 0.2% growth reported a year ago and suggests some stabilization in home improvement spending.

However, the composition of that growth is telling.

  • Comparable sales: +2.2%

  • Comparable customer transactions: -0.5%

  • Comparable average ticket: +3.0%

  • Average ticket: $93.09 versus $90.39 a year ago

In other words, customers are spending more when they visit Home Depot, but they're still visiting and buying less frequently. It looks more like inflation than a healthy consumer but there is some sequential improvement here. Transactions fell 1.6% in the same quarter last year, so the pace of decline has moderated considerably. Still, the recovery in spending is being driven by larger tickets rather than more transactions.

The company doesn't break down how much of the increase in average ticket comes from inflation, larger projects or customers purchasing more expensive products. That makes it difficult to draw conclusions about real consumption.

Another complication is Home Depot's growing professional contractor business, including its acquisitions of SRS Distribution and GMS. That business is increasingly important to total revenues but doesn't necessarily reflect the spending decisions of ordinary households.

Home Depot has been fighting a difficult housing market and is particularly exposed to interest rates. Elevated mortgage costs have kept homeowners locked into existing properties and depressed housing turnover, which is a major lever renovation and improvement spending.

On guidance, Home Depot now expects full-year comparable sales growth of 1.4% and adjusted earnings growth of approximately 2%. The earnings forecast implies adjusted EPS of roughly $14.98, slightly below the $15.05 analysts had expected.

The company also lowered its operating margin outlook to the bottom of its previous range, despite moving its total sales growth forecast to the top of the prior range.

That's a disappointing combination. Revenue rose 4.9% in the quarter but operating income increased just 2.4%, suggesting that stronger sales aren't translating into much additional profitability. I wonder if they start to pull on the price-hike lever, adding to consumer inflation.

For the US economic outlook, I would characterize the report as mildly encouraging but far from a signal that the consumer is roaring. Today's US retail sales report was also solid.

The slowdown in transaction declines is a positive sign and argues against a sharp deterioration in household spending. At the same time, the continued decline in traffic suggests consumers remain selective, particularly when it comes to expensive discretionary home improvement projects.

For now, though, the message is that the US consumer is holding up, but there is still considerable reluctance to spend. There might be more color in the call so I'll look out for details.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: NAHB housing market index for November 25 vs 29 estimate
item.description:
• Prior 29

Builder confidence weakens across all components, with current sales posting the largest decline.

  • The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell 4 points to 25 in November from 29 in October. That is the lowest reading over the past year and compares with 38 in November 2025.

The index remains well below the 50 level that separates positive from negative builder sentiment. The weakness is also broadening, with current sales, expectations for future sales and buyer traffic all moving lower.

The components showed:

  • Current single-family sales fell 6 points to 28 from 34.
  • Sales expectations for the next six months fell 2 points to 30 from 32.
  • Traffic of prospective buyers fell 2 points to 16 from 18.

The sharpest deterioration came in current sales. That component has fallen 11 points since August, suggesting builders are seeing conditions weaken as the year progresses.

Buyer traffic at 16 is another concern. Expectations for future sales are holding above assessments of current sales, but at 30, builders are hardly signaling confidence in a meaningful turnaround.

The regional data also showed declines across all four regions in November:

  • Northeast fell 6 points to 31.
  • Midwest fell 5 points to 30.
  • South fell 5 points to 23.
  • West fell 1 point to 19.

The three-month moving averages, which smooth out monthly volatility, reinforced the weaker trend. The Northeast fell to 34 from 38, the Midwest to 35 from 40, the South to 27 from 30 and the West to 23 from 26.

For the housing market, there is little encouragement in this report. Current sales are weakening, buyer traffic remains depressed, and expectations continue to move lower. Buyers need to show up before builders can become more confident. November’s numbers suggest that improvement remains elusive.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin is continuing the consolidation but sellers remain in control
item.description:
Sellers have controlled the technical breaks.

Going back to November 5, Bitcoin fell below its 100 and 200 hour moving averages and its 100 day moving average—all on the same day. That series of breaks shifted control firmly toward the sellers.

The sellers then leaned against the falling 100 hour moving average on November 9 and again on November 11. Buyers could not get above that moving average, and the subsequent break below the 200 day moving average—currently at $72,799—gave sellers another go-ahead to push lower.

They did.

The decline finally reached a low of $61,947 on Sunday. The price rebounded to $66,069 later that day before settling into a consolidation, with support developing near $63,815.

The 100 hour moving average is catching up.

The consolidation over the last two or so days has allowed the falling 100 hour moving average to catch up with the price. That moving average currently comes in at $65,654.

Today’s high reached $65,123, leaving the price $531 short of that technical barometer. However, with the moving average continuing to fall, decision time is getting closer for both buyers and sellers.

In the video, I outline why that moving average matters and the levels that would either keep sellers in control or give buyers an opportunity for a larger corrective move.

Stay below, and sellers keep the advantage.

As long as the price remains below the 100 hour moving average, sellers retain control. Buyers have stabilized the price after the sharp decline, but they still need to show they can take back a technical level.

On the downside, the levels to watch are:

  • $63,815: The consolidation floor. A break below would open the door for renewed selling.
  • $61,947: Sunday’s low and the next downside target if that floor gives way.

Holding support can slow a decline. Getting above resistance is what starts to change the bias.

What would give buyers more hope?

A move above the 100 hour moving average at $65,654—and the ability to stay above it—would give buyers their first meaningful technical improvement.

That would put the next upside targets in play:

  • $66,069: Sunday’s corrective high.
  • $69,265: The 38.2% retracement of the decline from the November high.
  • $69,460: The falling 200 hour moving average.

The retracement and 200 hour moving average form a higher resistance area. However, buyers first need to get through the 100 hour moving average and Sunday’s corrective high before that area becomes a more immediate focus.

The education: Consolidation gives the moving averages time to catch up.

After a sharp trend move, a market can correct through price, through time, or through a combination of both.

Bitcoin’s recent sideways trading is allowing the falling 100 hour moving average to move closer to the market. That creates a clearer decision point without requiring a large rally.

For sellers, the moving average becomes a level to lean against and define risk. Stay below, and the bearish bias remains intact. Move above and hold above, and some of that control starts to shift toward the buyers.

For buyers, a bounce from the low is a start. Breaking and holding above a moving average that has repeatedly capped rallies is stronger evidence of progress.

For now, the sellers remain in control. The 100 hour moving average is the barometer for a change.

Be aware. Be prepared.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
